title: Why you can't stop checking your phone
summary_es: Cómo están diseñadas las aplicaciones para retener nuestra atención y qué se puede hacer para recuperarla.
prediction_prompt: How many times a day do you think you look at your phone? What makes you pick it up?

sentences.text: Most of us like to believe that we decide how we spend our time.
The evidence, however, suggests otherwise.
The average adult now checks a phone around ninety times a day, often without knowing why.
This is not simply a lack of willpower.
It is the result of careful design.
Many of the most popular apps earn money from advertising, so their income depends on how long we stay.
As a result, companies employ teams of specialists whose only task is to keep us scrolling.
One of their most effective tools is the unpredictable reward.
When we pull down to refresh a page, we never know whether something interesting will appear.
Psychologists have known for decades that rewards which arrive at random are far harder to resist than regular ones.
Slot machines work in exactly the same way.
Another tool is the endless feed.
In the past, a newspaper or a television programme came to a natural end, which gave us a moment to decide what to do next.
Today, the next video starts automatically and the page never reaches the bottom, so that moment of decision has disappeared.
Notifications are another powerful technique.
A red dot or a short sound creates a small feeling of urgency, even when the message itself is trivial.
In one experiment, office workers who were interrupted by alerts took an average of twenty-three minutes to return to their original task.
What is more, they reported higher levels of stress, although they had completed the same amount of work.
Social approval plays a part as well.
Every like or comment tells us that other people have noticed us, and humans find this kind of attention extremely hard to ignore.
Teenagers appear to be especially sensitive to it, which may explain why they spend more time on social media than any other age group.
A former engineer at one large company has admitted that the like button was tested in dozens of versions before the most addictive one was chosen.
Not everyone accepts that technology is to blame.
Some researchers point out that every new medium, from the novel to television, was once accused of destroying our ability to concentrate.
They argue that people have always looked for distraction, and that phones merely make it easier to find.
There is some truth in this.
Nevertheless, earlier forms of entertainment were not redesigned every week on the basis of data about our behaviour.
So what can be done?
Experts tend to agree that relying on self-control alone rarely works.
It is more effective to change the environment.
Turning off all but the most essential notifications removes many of the triggers.
Keeping the phone in another room while working is surprisingly helpful, since even a silent phone on the desk reduces concentration.
Some people go further and switch their screens to black and white, which makes apps noticeably less attractive.
None of these measures requires us to give up technology.
The aim is rather to use it on purpose instead of by habit.
Attention, after all, is limited, and whatever we give it to becomes, in the end, our life.

language_focus.explanation_es: *However* y *Nevertheless* abren una frase nueva que contradice o matiza la anterior; *although* une las dos ideas dentro de la misma frase; *even when* añade un caso extremo. Fíjate en que *Nevertheless* (p5) responde a la objeción que el autor acaba de aceptar en parte.

language_focus.title_es: Which para comentar toda la idea anterior
language_focus.explanation_es: Tras una coma, *which* no se refiere a un nombre, sino a todo lo dicho antes: *…came to a natural end, which gave us a moment…* (lo cual nos daba un momento).

tasks.prompt: What is the writer's main point?

options.text: People today have far less willpower than previous generations did
Phones are built to hold our attention, but we can limit their effect
Technology companies should no longer be allowed to earn money from advertising
Using a phone at work is the main cause of stress

tasks.rationale_es: El texto explica que mirar el móvil es fruto de un diseño (p1) y termina proponiendo usarlo «a propósito y no por costumbre» (p7). No culpa a la falta de voluntad ni pide prohibir la publicidad.

tasks.prompt: Match paragraphs 2, 3 and 4 with the best heading. There is one extra heading.
tasks.rationale_es: P2 trata de las recompensas imprevisibles y del *feed* sin fin; p3, de las notificaciones y las interrupciones; p4, de la aprobación social. Ningún párrafo explica cómo ganar dinero en internet.

tasks.prompt: According to paragraph 2, why do app companies want people to stay longer?

options.text: Users pay a small amount for each hour
They want to collect more reviews from customers
Longer visits improve the design
They make money by showing adverts

tasks.rationale_es: Ganan dinero con la publicidad, así que sus ingresos dependen de cuánto tiempo nos quedamos.

options.text: unimportant
urgent
private
unexpected

tasks.rationale_es: *even when* marca un contraste: el aviso crea sensación de urgencia *aunque* el mensaje no la tenga, es decir, aunque sea insignificante.

tasks.prompt: The workers who were interrupted finished less work than the others.
tasks.rationale_es: Hicieron *the same amount of work*; lo que cambió fue el nivel de estrés.

tasks.prompt: Why does the writer mention slot machines?

options.text: To suggest that phones should be made illegal
To explain how apps earn their money
To show that gambling uses the same trick
To prove that rewards are always harmful

tasks.rationale_es: Acaba de explicar que las recompensas al azar son las más difíciles de resistir, y añade que las tragaperras funcionan «exactamente igual»: es una comparación, no una propuesta de prohibición.

tasks.prompt: What is the writer's attitude to the researchers mentioned in paragraph 5?

options.text: They are completely wrong about the past
They are partly right but miss a key difference
They are more convincing than the critics of technology
They do not understand history

tasks.rationale_es: *There is some truth in this* les da parte de razón; *Nevertheless* introduce la diferencia que pasan por alto: el entretenimiento de antes no se rediseñaba cada semana con datos.

tasks.prompt: Most teenagers would like to spend less time on social media.
tasks.rationale_es: El texto dice que los adolescentes pasan más tiempo que nadie en redes, pero no dice nada de lo que ellos querrían.

tasks.prompt: Which piece of advice does the writer NOT give?

options.text: Keep your phone in a different room
Switch off most notifications
Change the screen to black and white
Delete social media apps completely

tasks.rationale_es: Los otros tres consejos están en el párrafo 6. El autor deja claro que no hace falta renunciar a la tecnología (p7).

tasks.prompt: In paragraph 5, what does "this" refer to in "There is some truth in this"?

options.text: The claim that novels destroyed concentration
The fact that phones are redesigned every week
The view that humans never stopped seeking ways to escape
The belief that every new technology is harmful to society

tasks.rationale_es: *This* recoge el argumento de la frase anterior: siempre hemos buscado distracción y el móvil solo lo pone más fácil.

tasks.prompt: Complete the summary with one word from the text in each gap.
tasks.text: Apps keep us hooked with rewards that arrive at {{1}} and with alerts that create a feeling of {{2}}.
tasks.rationale_es: *rewards which arrive at random* (p2) y *a small feeling of urgency* (p3).

tasks.prompt: On average, how many minutes did interrupted workers need to return to their task?
tasks.rationale_es: *an average of twenty-three minutes*: veintitrés minutos de media.
